questions.q: A 32-year-old male with HIV presents with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy but remains completely asymptomatic otherwise. His CD4 count is 450 cells/µL. According to WHO clinical staging, what is his current stage?
opts: Clinical Stage 1
Clinical Stage 2
Clinical Stage 3
Clinical Stage 4
questions.exp: WHO Clinical Stage 1 is characterized by asymptomatic disease or persistent generalized lymphadenopathy (PGL) alone, regardless of CD4 count at this classification level. The absence of other systemic symptoms or opportunistic infections defines this early stage despite the CD4 count being above 500 cells/µL.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with a 1.5 cm seborrheic keratosis on the forearm. You decide to treat it with cryotherapy. Which cryogen would provide the most effective tissue destruction while minimizing the risk of incomplete treatment?
opts: Nitrous oxide (N₂O) via closed probe system
Liquid nitrogen (LN₂) via spray canister
Dimethyl ether and propane (DMEP) via handheld applicator
Carbon dioxide dry ice via cotton applicator
questions.exp: Liquid nitrogen at -195.8°C to -196°C is the most effective and widely used cryogen in dermatologic surgery for both benign and malignant lesions. While DMEP (-50°C to -57°C) and N₂O (-88°C to -89°C) are less effective, LN₂'s superior temperature capacity ensures rapid freezing necessary for maximal tissue destruction. CO₂ dry ice at -78.5°C is also less effective than LN₂.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman develops primary pulmonary sporotrichosis after inhalation of fungal conidia while working in a contaminated grain storage facility. Histological examination of tissue biopsies reveals yeast cells surrounded by a thick, star-shaped, radiating eosinophilic matrix. What immune components compose this characteristic structure?
opts: IgA and IgE antibodies only
IgM and IgG antibodies
Complement cascade proteins only
Fibrin and polymorphonuclear leukocytes
questions.exp: The asteroid body, representing the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon, is composed of deposited IgM and IgG antibodies that form an antigen-antibody complex designed to protect yeast cells from host phagocytes. While similar Splendore-Hoeppli phenomena can occur in other deep infections, the specific immunological composition in sporotrichosis involves these immunoglobulin classes.

questions.q: A 3-month-old premature female infant (birth weight 800 g) presents with a bright red nodule on the cheek that has been enlarging since 6 weeks of age. On histopathology and immunohistochemistry, the lesion shows proliferating endothelial cells with strong and diffuse positivity for GLUT1. Which of the following best explains the universal GLUT1 positivity in this lesion?
opts: GLUT1 is expressed only during the proliferative phase of infantile haemangioma development
GLUT1 is an erythrocyte-type glucose transporter expressed throughout all phases of infantile haemangioma life cycle, distinguishing it from vascular malformations
GLUT1 expression indicates malignant transformation of the haemangioma
GLUT1 positivity is specific to congenital haemangiomas and helps differentiate them from infantile haemangiomas
questions.exp: GLUT1 is the definitive hallmark of infantile haemangiomas, expressed consistently by tumour endothelial cells throughout proliferating, involuting, and involuted phases. This sustained expression across all life cycle stages distinguishes IH as true benign vascular neoplasms from vascular malformations and congenital haemangiomas, which are GLUT1-negative. The persistent GLUT1 positivity reflects the neoplastic nature of cellular hyperplasia inherent to IH.

questions.q: A 5-day-old neonate presents with 1-2 cm flaccid bullae on the diaper area that rupture within 24-48 hours, leaving golden-yellow crusts with a peripheral collarette of scale. The Nikolsky sign is negative and mucous membranes are spared. Which desmosomal protein is the target of the exfoliative toxins responsible for this condition?
opts: Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3)
Desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
Desmocollin 1 (Dsc1)
Envoplakin
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo of the newborn is mediated by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins (ETA or ETB) that cleave desmoglein 1, a desmosomal cadherin responsible for keratinocyte adhesion in the superficial epidermis. The cleavage occurs subcorneally within the stratum granulosum, creating the characteristic flaccid bullae with negative Nikolsky sign.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a newborn's DIAPER CASTLE where 1 (Dsg1) GOLDEN-YELLOW guards protect the SUPERFICIAL moat—when exotoxins breach it, the castle's desmosome LADDER (desmoglein 1 rungs) snaps at the SUBCORNEAL rampart, leaving behind a COLLARETTE CROWN of scale debris.

questions.q: A mother brings her 2-week-old full-term neonate for routine examination. On inspection of the face, you observe multiple uniform pinpoint to 2 mm yellow papules clustered over the nose, cheeks, and forehead at the follicular ostia. The infant is asymptomatic. What is the most likely diagnosis and underlying mechanism?
opts: Milia due to retention of keratin within epidermis
Neonatal sebaceous gland hyperplasia secondary to transplacental maternal androgens
Neonatal cephalic pustulosis caused by Malassezia furfur
Miliaria crystallina from eccrine sweat duct obstruction
questions.exp: Neonatal sebaceous gland hyperplasia presents as yellow/yellowish-white macules and papules at follicular ostia on the central face, affecting 50–89% of term neonates. The condition is driven by transplacental transfer of maternal androgens, which stimulate fetal sebaceous glands to produce sebum at adult rates; glands involute as maternal androgens clear by 4–6 months. The key distinguishing feature from milia is the yellow colour and location at the ostia, versus pearly-white cysts in milia.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Physiological, Pigmentary and Mechanical Neonatal Lesions
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a GOLDEN BABY FACE (yellow sebaceous papules) covered in MOTHER'S HORMONE MIST (maternal androgens) settling on the NOSE & CHEEKS like a treasure map of follicles—when the mist clears at month 6, the gold vanishes.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male farmer from Brazil presents with a slowly progressive nodule on his foot following a puncture wound sustained while working in the field. A tissue biopsy reveals melanized fungal hyphae. What is the most likely causative organism?
opts: Exophiala jeanselmei
Cladophialophora bantiana
Sporothrix schenckii
Talaromyces marneffei
questions.exp: Exophiala jeanselmei is the most common causative organism of phaeohyphomycosis, particularly in subcutaneous infections following traumatic implantation. Cladophialophora bantiana is specifically associated with cerebral phaeohyphomycosis, not localized subcutaneous disease. The combination of localized subcutaneous presentation with traumatic inoculation from soil/plants in a tropical region points to E. jeanselmei.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture EXOPHIALA climbing the FARMER'S BOOT on a Brazilian plantation—the most common culprit sneaking through puncture wounds in muddy fields.

questions.q: A 31-week premature male infant is born with profoundly rigid, tightly adherent skin, severe microstomia, and absent eyebrows. Chest imaging reveals pulmonary hypoplasia. What is the most common genetic mutation underlying this presentation of restrictive dermopathy?
opts: Homozygous null mutations in ZMPSTE24 gene
De novo heterozygous mutations in LMNA gene
Autosomal dominant inheritance of COL1A1 mutations
X-linked recessive mutations in SLC9A3R1 gene
questions.exp:
Restrictive dermopathy (RD) is classified into two molecular subtypes; ZMPSTE24-mutated RD represents the vast majority of classical cases and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. ZMPSTE24 encodes a zinc metallopeptidase responsible for processing farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A; deficiency causes toxic accumulation at the nuclear envelope. The primary laminopathy caused by LMNA mutations is much rarer.
🏰 Palace: Picture a ZIPPING enzyme (ZMPSTE24) working on a FACTORY ASSEMBLY LINE—when broken, toxic FARNESYLATED PRELAMIN builds up like jamming gears, shutting down the NUCLEAR FACTORY in the embryo's dermis.

questions.q: A term neonate born to a mother with poor perineal hygiene develops pustules in the umbilical region within 48 hours, which progress over 3 days to widespread tissue-paper-like wrinkled erythema with flexural accentuation, fever, and extreme cutaneous tenderness. Culture from the umbilical stump grows Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. Which of the following best explains the progression from localized to generalized disease in this case?
opts: Local bacterial overgrowth at the primary focus with increasing toxin concentration
Hematogenous dissemination of exfoliative toxins (particularly ETB) from an occult primary focus of infection
Progressive epidermal thickness leading to deeper subcorneal cleavage planes
Mutation of the staphylococcal strain from toxin-producing to invasive phenotype
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS, or Ritter's disease in neonates) represents the generalized form of the same toxin-mediated disease spectrum. While bullous impetigo remains localized due to local toxin production, SSSS occurs when exfoliative toxins (especially ETB encoded on plasmids) diffuse from a distant, often occult primary site and spread hematogenously, causing widespread intraepidermal cleavage at the stratum granulosum.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine the UMBILICAL STUMP as a HIDDEN FORTRESS where ETB toxin grenades are launched into the BLOODSTREAM HIGHWAY—they travel kingdom-wide, triggering TISSUE-PAPER WRINKLED collapse of the SUPERFICIAL EPIDERMIS everywhere (flexural first), like a systemic SABOTAGE spreading from one hidden castle.

questions.q: According to the UK Working Party Diagnostic Criteria, which of the following is the mandatory feature required for diagnosis of atopic dermatitis?
opts: Onset of disease below age 2 years
History of flexural involvement
An itchy skin condition in the last 12 months
Visible flexural dermatitis on physical examination
questions.exp: The UK Working Party Diagnostic Criteria mandate the presence of itchy skin in the last 12 months as the obligatory feature, along with three or more additional criteria. All other options are supplementary criteria, not mandatory.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: The ITCHY PRINCE (mandatory) sits on the THRONE in the grand hall—you MUST pass through his itching chamber to enter the castle; three guards (flexural, dry skin, atopic history) stand ready at the gates.

questions.q: During cryotherapy treatment, a dermatologist applies liquid nitrogen to a wart with a rapid freeze technique but then allows the tissue to thaw quickly at room temperature. Based on tissue destruction mechanisms, which outcome would be most likely?
opts: Enhanced intracellular ice crystal formation and recrystallization damage
Incomplete tissue destruction due to suboptimal solute effect and recrystallization
Accelerated microvascular thrombosis within 24-48 hours
Maximal ischemic necrosis through prolonged vascular stasis
questions.exp: The fundamental principle of cryosurgery is rapid freeze followed by SLOW thaw. A rapid thaw prevents the destructive 'solute effect' and recrystallization phase where small ice crystals fuse into larger, more damaging crystals. The slow thaw phase is critical for maximizing tissue destruction; rapid thawing negates this essential mechanism.

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome (port-wine stain + venous malformation + limb hypertrophy, all slow-flow) is evaluated for potential hemodynamic complications. Which ONE clinical finding would immediately shift the diagnosis from KTS to Parkes-Weber syndrome?
opts: Progressive limb overgrowth and increased limb girth over 2 years
Detection of a palpable arterial thrill and audible continuous bruit over the affected limb
Development of lymphatic vesicles overlying the port-wine stain
Onset of limb-length discrepancy coinciding with the start of weight-bearing
questions.exp: The critical diagnostic distinction between Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome and Parkes-Weber syndrome is hemodynamic: KTS is strictly slow-flow (capillary-lymphatic-venous malformations), while Parkes-Weber syndrome is characterized by underlying high-flow arteriovenous fistulae or malformations. The presence of an arterial thrill (palpable vibration) and continuous (machinery) bruit indicates arterial involvement, which is the MANDATORY criterion for Parkes-Weber and excludes KTS.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: KTS girls sip slow WINE (slow-flow) at the castle banquet hall peacefully—but if a THRILL and BRUIT (WHOOOOSH like a trumpet) arrive, a fast ARTERIAL PRINCE (Parkes-Weber) has crashed the party. Thrill = No more KTS!

questions.q: Which characteristic feature of dematiaceous fungi contributes to their disease-causing potential and distinguishes them from other pathogenic fungi?
opts: Production of ergot alkaloids in their cell walls
Presence of melanin in their cell walls
Ability to produce heat-shock proteins at body temperature
Secretion of chitinase enzymes into the bloodstream
questions.exp: Dematiaceous fungi are characterized by the presence of melanin in their cell walls, which gives them their characteristic dark, pigmented appearance and provides the term 'phaeo' (dark color) in phaeohyphomycosis. This melanin is a key virulence factor that may assist in immune evasion and protection. The other options describe features not specific to or associated with dematiaceous fungi.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Dark MELANIN PIGMENT coats the fungal CASTLE WALLS like a protective shield—melanin makes dematiaceous fungi the 'dark knights' of mycosis.

questions.q: A 3-month-old male infant presents with sparse, depigmented, lusterless hair that feels coarse and brittle like steel wool. His skin is notably doughy and pale with generalized hypopigmentation. Serum copper levels are markedly decreased. Which enzyme deficiency is MOST directly responsible for the characteristic hair and skin depigmentation in this condition?
opts: Lysyl oxidase
Tyrosinase
Cytochrome c oxidase
Ascorbic acid oxidase
questions.exp: Tyrosinase is the copper-dependent enzyme responsible for melanin synthesis. Its deficiency in Menkes disease due to systemic copper depletion causes the characteristic depigmented, lusterless hair and generalized hypopigmentation of the skin. Lysyl oxidase affects collagen cross-linking, cytochrome c oxidase causes neurodegeneration, and ascorbic acid oxidase affects bone metabolism.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male gardener from Brazil presents with nodular lesions along his forearm following a thorn prick while pruning roses. Culture at 25°C reveals thin, septate hyaline hyphae with conidia arranged in a characteristic palmate, flower-like bouquet pattern. Which *Sporothrix* species is MOST likely responsible for this classic presentation?
opts: *Sporothrix brasiliensis*
*Sporothrix schenckii* sensu stricto
*Sporothrix globosa*
*Sporothrix mexicana*
questions.exp: *Sporothrix schenckii* sensu stricto is the classical organism originally described in sporotrichosis infections and presents with the typical lymphocutaneous form following traumatic inoculation. While *S. brasiliensis* is highly virulent and endemic to Brazil, it is specifically associated with zoonotic transmission via cat bites and scratches rather than plant trauma alone.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a geographic port-wine stain over his left lower limb, varicose veins, and progressive soft-tissue hypertrophy of that limb. Clinical examination reveals NO palpable arterial thrill or audible bruit. Which genetic mechanism BEST explains this presentation?
opts: Germline heterozygous RASA1 mutation causing loss of neurofibromin function
Postzygotic somatic gain-of-function PIK3CA mutation causing constitutive PI3K/AKT/mTOR hyperactivation
High-flow arteriovenous fistulae due to VEGF-A overexpression in the affected limb
Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in VHL causing widespread angioma formation
questions.exp: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome is driven by postzygotic gain-of-function PIK3CA mutations (p110α), which constitutively activate the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway—the master regulator of growth, proliferation, and vascular development. This results in the classic triad of capillary malformation, venous malformation, and progressive limb overgrowth. Critically, the absence of an arterial thrill or bruit excludes high-flow arteriovenous fistulae, ruling out Parkes-Weber syndrome. The mutation is somatically mosaic and postzygotic, explaining why it is sporadic and non-heritable.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A giant PI3K cake (shaped like a castle tower) is OVERGROWTH-decorated, spreading across the left limb platform—but NO arterial pipes (no thrill/bruit) run through the kitchen. The mutation is a MOSAIC TILE floor, not passed down the royal bloodline.

questions.q: An infested patient's apartment is being treated for bed bugs. The exterminator notes that despite aggressive treatment, complete eradication is extremely challenging. Which biological feature of adult Cimex lectularius most directly explains the difficulty in achieving rapid pest control?
opts: All five nymphal instars require blood meals to moult, prolonging the life cycle
Adults can survive an average of 70 days and up to one year without a blood meal in ideal conditions
Females lay approximately 300 pearly white eggs cemented into crevices every 10 days
Bed bugs are strictly nocturnal and hidden in dark crevices during daylight hours
questions.exp: Adult bed bugs possess extreme starvation resistance, surviving an average of 70 days without feeding and potentially up to one year under optimal conditions. This remarkable longevity without a host makes eradication difficult because dormant adults can persist through periods when pesticides are not applied or between treatments.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine an adult bed bug in a LOCKED CASTLE CRYPT for an ENTIRE YEAR, sipping from an invisible IV of stored blood, wearing a monk's robe—it simply refuses to starve and emerge for poison.

questions.q: A preterm female infant with restrictive dermopathy is noted to have a carrier frequency of 1 in 21 in her ethnic population. Which ancestral group shows this exceptionally high carrier status for RD?
opts: Ashkenazi Jewish populations in Eastern Europe
Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite and Hutterite populations in North America
Scandinavian populations in Northern Europe
Sub-Saharan African populations in West Africa
questions.exp:
Restrictive dermopathy occurs globally but demonstrates a marked founder effect in specific populations. A shared founder mutation is highly prevalent in the Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite and Hutterite populations of North America, where carrier status is exceptionally high (estimated up to 1 in 21 in Hutterite populations from South Dakota).
🏰 Palace: Imagine a HUTTERITE VILLAGE in SOUTH DAKOTA with 21 houses—ONE contains a FOUNDER MUTATION passed down through generations like a FAMILY HEIRLOOM, creating carriers who walk with RIGID SKIN.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient presents with nocturnal pruritic lesions on exposed skin. Physical examination reveals linear clusters of papules on the arms and neck. The patient reports the bites are completely painless and only notices them upon waking. Which morphological and behavioral feature of the causative organism best explains the painless nature of the bite?
opts: Wingless, dorsoventrally flattened body structure allowing deep penetration
Saliva containing potent anaesthetic and anticoagulant compounds
Piercing-sucking mouthparts adapted for vascular puncture
Extreme starvation resistance enabling prolonged feeding episodes
questions.exp: Bed bug saliva contains both anaesthetic and anticoagulant agents that prevent pain sensation and allow uninterrupted blood feeding, which is why hosts remain asleep during the 3–12 minute feeding period. The anaesthetic component specifically numbs the bite site, while the anticoagulant prevents clotting.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a bed bug INJECTING LIQUID NOVOCAIN (anaesthetic) and BLOOD-THINNING MEDICINE from a hospital IV bag directly into the sleeper's arm—the guest doesn't feel a thing and keeps snoring while the vampire feasts.

questions.q: A newborn screening identifies multiple small haemangiomas across the trunk in a miliary pattern, and ultrasound reveals hepatic involvement. The infant is a 29-week gestational age female with a birth weight of 950 g. Based on epidemiological risk factors, which statement is most accurate regarding this presentation?
opts: Prematurity and low birth weight do not increase infantile haemangioma risk; the female predominance alone explains this case

The incidence of infantile haemangiomas in infants <1000 g is 25–30%, and female infants <2500 g have a 2:1 to 5:1 higher risk, making multifocal disease with extracutaneous involvement a recognized presentation
This multifocal pattern is a benign variant that never requires systemic therapy and always involutes spontaneously by age 5
Birth weight >1000 g is protective, but advanced maternal age significantly increases haemangioma risk regardless of prematurity
questions.exp: Infantile haemangiomas show a striking association with prematurity and low birth weight; infants weighing <1000 g have a 25–30% incidence, far exceeding the 4–5% population baseline. The female-to-male ratio of 2:1 to 5:1 compounds this risk. Multifocal infantile haemangiomas with hepatic involvement (historically called diffuse neonatal hemangiomatosis) represent a recognized clinical presentation requiring careful assessment for systemic manifestations and consideration of systemic therapy.

questions.q: Which gene mutation is considered the hallmark genetic discovery in atopic dermatitis pathogenesis, affecting epidermal barrier function?
opts: TNF-α gene on chromosome 6
Filaggrin (FLG) gene on chromosome 1q21
IL-4 receptor gene on chromosome 16
TSLP gene on chromosome 5q22
questions.exp: Loss-of-function mutations in the Filaggrin (FLG) gene, encoded within the epidermal differentiation complex on chromosome 1q21, represent the hallmark genetic discovery in AD. Filaggrin is a critical component of keratohyalin granules essential for barrier function.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: A FILTHY FLAGGED (FLG) gate on CHROMOSOME 1 QUEUE-21 crumbles, collapsing the castle's protective BRICK WALL barrier—the fortress falls to invading allergens and irritants.

questions.q: A male infant with X-linked Menkes disease caused by ATP7A gene mutation presents with systemic copper deficiency. The mutation prevents normal function of the copper-transporting ATPase. At which anatomical site does this transporter normally function to export copper into the portal circulation?
opts: Hepatic sinusoidal membrane
Intestinal mucosa brush border
Blood-brain barrier endothelium
Renal proximal tubule epithelium
questions.exp: The ATP7A gene encodes a P-type ATPase that normally exports copper from intestinal mucosa into the portal circulation. Mutations in ATP7A prevent this copper export, trapping copper in intestinal brush border cells and causing profound systemic copper deficiency affecting multiple organ systems.

questions.q: A 3-day-old African neonatal presents with extensive blue-grey macular patches over the lumbosacral region and buttocks. The mother is concerned about bruising from labour. Dermoscopy shows a homogeneous blue-grey discoloration in the dermis without surface change. What is the pathophysiological basis for the distinctive colour of this lesion?
opts: Oxygenated haemoglobin in superficial dermal capillaries causing central cyanosis
The Tyndall effect—deep dermal melanin absorbs longer wavelengths and reflects scattered shorter blue/violet wavelengths
Extravascular red blood cells undergoing oxidation to methaemoglobin in the dermis
Copper deposition in dermal fibroblasts from maternal transplacental transfer
questions.exp: Mongolian spots (congenital dermal melanocytosis) are caused by ectopic melanocytes retained deep in the dermis due to incomplete neural crest migration. The characteristic blue-grey appearance results from the Tyndall effect: melanin at depth absorbs longer (red/orange/yellow) wavelengths and allows reflection of scattered shorter (blue/violet) wavelengths, creating the blue-grey optical illusion. This condition is present in 90–100% of Asian and Black neonates but <10% of White infants and involutes over years.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Physiological, Pigmentary and Mechanical Neonatal Lesions
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Deep in the CASTLE DUNGEON (dermis), MELANIN KNIGHTS stand at the gates—they SWALLOW the RED & YELLOW invaders (long wavelengths) but BOUNCE BACK the BLUE GUARDS (short wavelengths), making the dungeon glow BLUE-GREY like Tyndall's enchanted mirror.

questions.q: A patient with HIV and a CD4 count of 75 cells/µL presents with visual floaters and photopsia. Which opportunistic infection is most characteristic at this CD4 threshold and clinical presentation?
opts: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis
Cryptococcal meningitis
Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC)
questions.exp: CMV retinitis presents with visual symptoms (floaters, photopsia, visual field defects) and occurs at very low CD4 counts (<50 cells/µL is highest risk, but can occur at <100). The visual presentation combined with the extremely low CD4 count of 75 cells/µL makes CMV retinitis the most likely diagnosis among the options.
